Protein Basket respects your privacy. This policy explains what we collect when you contact us or buy from us, and what we do with it.

WHAT WE COLLECT
When you send an enquiry through this website, message us on WhatsApp or call us, we collect the details you choose to give: your name, phone number, email address if you provide one, and the details of what you are asking about or ordering.

HOW WE USE IT
We use your details only to answer your enquiry, to prepare and hand over your order, and to contact you about that order. If you ask us to, we may also message you about new stock or offers; you can tell us to stop at any time and we will.

WHO WE SHARE IT WITH
We do not sell your information, and we do not share it with anyone for marketing. If an order has to be delivered, we share only the name, address and phone number the delivery needs.

HEALTH INFORMATION
If you tell us about a health condition while asking for advice, we use it only to answer your question.

PAYMENTS
We never ask for card numbers, UPI PINs, OTPs or bank passwords over the phone, on WhatsApp or through this website. If anyone claiming to be Protein Basket asks you for one, do not share it.

YOUR CHOICES
You can ask us what information we hold about you, ask us to correct it, or ask us to delete it. Message us on WhatsApp at +91 98238 78057, email basketprotein@gmail.com, or visit the store.

PRODUCTS
We sell food supplements made by other companies. Descriptions, nutrition information, serving sizes and directions come from the manufacturer and are printed on each pack; the pack is the final word. The photographs on this website are of products on our shelves, but flavours, sizes and packaging change, so please confirm exactly what you are buying before you pay.

PRICES
Prices change with brand offers and pack sizes, so we confirm the price at the time you buy, in the store or on WhatsApp. A price is not fixed until we have confirmed your order.

ORDERS AND STOCK
Stock moves quickly. If an item sells out after you have asked for it, we will tell you and suggest an alternative, or you can wait for fresh stock.

CHECK YOUR PRODUCT
Please check the seal, batch number, expiry date and MRP when you receive a product, and before you open it. Because supplements are consumable, tell us about any problem with a sealed product straight away and before opening it, so we can put it right with you.

HEALTH
Supplements are not medicines and are not intended to diagnose, treat, cure or prevent any disease. Advice we give in the store or on WhatsApp is general guidance, not medical advice. If you have a medical condition, take regular medication, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or are under 18, speak to a doctor before using any supplement. Always follow the manufacturer's directions and do not exceed the stated dose.

ALLERGIES
Many supplements contain milk, soy, egg, nuts or gluten, or are made in facilities that handle them. Read the allergen information on the pack before you buy.

THIS WEBSITE
We try to keep the information here accurate, but it may not always reflect today's stock or packaging. The guides on this site are general information, not personal advice.

Protein Basket respects your privacy. This policy explains what we collect when you contact us or buy from us, and what we do with it.

WHAT WE COLLECT
When you send an enquiry through this website, message us on WhatsApp or call us, we collect the details you choose to give: your name, phone number, email address if you provide one, and the details of what you are asking about or ordering.

HOW WE USE IT
We use your details only to answer your enquiry, to prepare and hand over your order, and to contact you about that order. If you ask us to, we may also message you about new stock or offers; you can tell us to stop at any time and we will.

WHO WE SHARE IT WITH
We do not sell your information, and we do not share it with anyone for marketing. If an order has to be delivered, we share only the name, address and phone number the delivery needs.

HEALTH INFORMATION
If you tell us about a health condition while asking for advice, we use it only to answer your question.

PAYMENTS
We never ask for card numbers, UPI PINs, OTPs or bank passwords over the phone, on WhatsApp or through this website. If anyone claiming to be Protein Basket asks you for one, do not share it.

YOUR CHOICES
You can ask us what information we hold about you, ask us to correct it, or ask us to delete it. Message us on WhatsApp at +91 98238 78057, email basketprotein@gmail.com, or visit the store.

CONTACT
Protein Basket, Shop No. 2, Chintamani Complex, Ring Road, near Manjiri Textile, Pratap Nagar, Nagpur, Maharashtra 440022.

These terms apply when you buy from Protein Basket — in our store in Pratap Nagar, Nagpur, over WhatsApp, or after an enquiry through this website.

PRODUCTS
We sell food supplements made by other companies. Descriptions, nutrition information, serving sizes and directions come from the manufacturer and are printed on each pack; the pack is the final word. The photographs on this website are of products on our shelves, but flavours, sizes and packaging change, so please confirm exactly what you are buying before you pay.

PRICES
Prices change with brand offers and pack sizes, so we confirm the price at the time you buy, in the store or on WhatsApp. A price is not fixed until we have confirmed your order.

ORDERS AND STOCK
Stock moves quickly. If an item sells out after you have asked for it, we will tell you and suggest an alternative, or you can wait for fresh stock.

CHECK YOUR PRODUCT
Please check the seal, batch number, expiry date and MRP when you receive a product, and before you open it. Because supplements are consumable, tell us about any problem with a sealed product straight away and before opening it, so we can put it right with you.

HEALTH
Supplements are not medicines and are not intended to diagnose, treat, cure or prevent any disease. Advice we give in the store or on WhatsApp is general guidance, not medical advice. If you have a medical condition, take regular medication, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or are under 18, speak to a doctor before using any supplement. Always follow the manufacturer's directions and do not exceed the stated dose.

ALLERGIES
Many supplements contain milk, soy, egg, nuts or gluten, or are made in facilities that handle them. Read the allergen information on the pack before you buy.

THIS WEBSITE
We try to keep the information here accurate, but it may not always reflect today's stock or packaging. The guides on this site are general information, not personal advice.

props.sub: Both come from milk and both do the same basic job. The difference is how much the protein has been filtered — and what that means for your goal and your budget.

props.heading: Whey concentrate or whey isolate: which should you buy?
props.body:
Walk along any supplement shelf and the two words you will see most are "whey" and "isolate". Both come from milk, both are complete proteins, and both do the same basic job: they make it easy to add protein to your day. The difference is how much the protein has been filtered.

WHEY CONCENTRATE
Most tubs labelled simply "whey protein" are a concentrate, or a blend with some concentrate in it. It is filtered less, so it keeps a little more of milk's natural carbohydrate (lactose) and fat. Per scoop that usually means slightly less protein and slightly more calories than an isolate — and a lower price. For most people training a few times a week, a good concentrate is all they need.

WHEY ISOLATE
An isolate is filtered further. That typically pushes the protein share of each scoop higher and brings the lactose, carbohydrate and fat down. People tend to choose one when:
• dairy sits heavy — many people who find milk uncomfortable manage an isolate better, though it is not lactose-free unless the label says so;
• they are cutting and counting every calorie;
• they simply want the most protein per scoop.
The trade-off is price: an isolate usually costs more for the same weight.

HOW TO CHOOSE
Start with your goal and your budget, not the label on the front.
• Building muscle on a budget — a concentrate or a blend does the job.
• Cutting, or dairy bothers you — an isolate is worth the extra cost.
• Just trying to eat more protein — either works; pick a flavour you will actually drink.

READ THE BACK OF THE TUB
The front of a tub is marketing. The nutrition panel on the back tells you what you are paying for: protein per serving, the serving size, and how many servings are in the pack. Divide the price by the number of servings to compare two tubs fairly.

props.heading: Creatine, explained: what it does, how to take it, and the myths
props.body:
Creatine is one of the most researched supplements in sport, and one of the most misunderstood at the gym. Here is what it is, how people take it, and the myths worth ignoring.

WHAT IT IS
Creatine is a compound your body already makes, and it is also found in meat and fish. Your muscles use it to regenerate energy during short, hard efforts — a heavy set, a sprint. Taking it as a supplement tops up those stores, which is why it is popular with people who lift weights.

MONOHYDRATE OR HCL?
Creatine monohydrate is the form most of the research has been done on, and it is usually the best value. "Micronised" monohydrate is simply milled finer so it mixes more easily. Creatine HCL is a different form sold in smaller doses; some people prefer it, but it typically costs more per serving.

HOW PEOPLE TAKE IT
Most people take a small daily dose — follow the serving size on the label — mixed into water, juice or a protein shake. Taking it consistently matters more than the time of day. Some people start with a higher "loading" dose for a few days; it is optional, and the label gives the manufacturer's recommendation. Drink enough water through the day.

MYTHS WORTH IGNORING
• "It is a steroid." It is not. It is a nutritional supplement.
• "You have to cycle it." Many people take it continuously; there is no need to stop and start unless your doctor advises it.
• "The weight you gain is fat." Early weight gain on creatine is mostly water held in the muscle.

WHO SHOULD CHECK WITH A DOCTOR FIRST
Anyone with kidney disease or another medical condition, anyone on regular medication, anyone pregnant or breastfeeding, and anyone under 18 should speak to a doctor before taking creatine.

props.heading: How to tell a genuine supplement from a fake
props.body:
Fake and tampered supplements are a real problem in India, and they are often sold at a price that seems too good to be true. The good news: most genuine products give you several ways to check them. Here is what to look at before you pay.

1. THE SEAL
A genuine tub has an intact seal under the lid — usually a foil or induction seal — and often a tamper-evident band around the lid itself. If the seal is loose, torn or re-glued, do not accept it.

2. THE LABEL AND PRINT QUALITY
Look for blurred printing, spelling mistakes, colours that look off, or a label peeling at the edges. Big brands print cleanly.

3. BATCH NUMBER, DATES AND MRP
Every pack should show a batch or lot number, a manufacturing date, a best-before or expiry date, and the MRP. Check that the dates make sense and that the batch number is printed, not handwritten.

4. THE FSSAI LICENCE
Food supplements sold in India should carry an FSSAI licence number on the label. Imported products should also carry the importer's name and address.

5. THE BRAND'S OWN AUTHENTICITY CHECK
Many brands now print a scratch code, QR code or unique number you can verify on their website or app. If the pack has one, use it — it takes a minute.

6. THE PRICE
Supplements do go on offer, but a price far below what everyone else charges is the most common sign that something is wrong.

7. THE PRODUCT ITSELF
Genuine powder mixes and smells the way it did last time. Lumps that will not break, an odd smell or a strange taste are reasons to stop and ask.

AT PROTEIN BASKET
Every tub we sell carries its manufacturer seal, batch number and printed MRP, and you are welcome to check all of it at the counter before you pay — scratch codes included. Customers mention genuine products in our Google reviews, and we would like to keep it that way.

If you are ever unsure about a product — ours or anyone else's — bring it in, or send us a photo on WhatsApp, and we will tell you what we see.

props.heading: Protein for vegetarians: getting enough on an Indian diet
props.body:
A lot of vegetarian diets in India fall short on protein — not because the food is poor, but because the usual plate is built around rice and roti. Here is how to get more from food first, and where a supplement can help.

HOW MUCH DO YOU NEED?
It varies with your body weight, age and how active you are, and people who lift weights regularly usually aim higher. A doctor or dietitian can give you a number for your own body; this guide is about getting there.

PROTEIN FROM THE KITCHEN
Good vegetarian sources you probably already eat:
• Paneer and tofu
• Curd, hung curd and milk
• Dal, rajma, chole and other pulses
• Soya chunks
• Peanuts, other nuts and seeds
The easiest change is adding a protein source to every meal rather than trying to fix it all at dinner — curd with lunch, a bowl of dal beside the sabzi, paneer or soya a few times a week.

WHERE A SUPPLEMENT FITS
If you are training hard or struggling to eat enough, a scoop of protein is simply a convenient way to close the gap. Whey — both concentrate and isolate — is made from milk, so it suits vegetarians who take dairy. It is not vegan.

ONE THING TO CHECK
Not every protein on the shelf is vegetarian. Egg-white (albumen) proteins, such as Venky's Albumen Plus, are made from eggs, and some capsules use gelatin. Look for the green vegetarian dot on the pack, and ask us if you are not sure.

A SIMPLE DAY THAT WORKS
Breakfast: poha or upma with a glass of milk or a bowl of curd.
Lunch: roti, dal and paneer sabzi.
Evening: roasted chana or peanuts — and a protein shake if you have trained.
Dinner: rajma or chole with rice, and a salad with soya or tofu.

We are happy to help you choose a vegetarian protein at the counter.

A note on health: supplements are not medicines. If you have a medical condition, take regular medication, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or are under 18, speak to your doctor before you start.

props.heading: Mass gainer or whey protein? Choosing by your goal
props.body:
Mass gainers and whey protein sit next to each other on the shelf and look alike, but they are built for different people.

WHAT A MASS GAINER IS
A gainer is mostly carbohydrate with protein added, and some fat. One serving can carry several hundred calories — the label tells you exactly how many. It exists for one job: helping people who struggle to eat enough to put on weight.

WHAT WHEY IS
Whey protein is mostly protein, with relatively few calories per scoop. It adds protein to your day without adding much else.

WHICH ONE IS FOR YOU?
Choose a gainer if you are naturally thin, have a small appetite, and find it genuinely hard to eat enough — the classic "hard gainer".
Choose whey if you already eat enough food and want more protein, or you are trying to stay lean or lose fat.
The common mistake is buying a gainer when you do not need the extra calories. A gainer on top of a full diet mostly adds fat.

USING A GAINER SENSIBLY
• Start with a smaller serving than the label's full dose, and see how your stomach handles it.
• Use it as well as meals, not instead of them.
• Train. The calories are meant to fuel growth from lifting, not replace it.

A HALF-WAY OPTION
Some people make their own: a scoop of whey blended with milk, a banana, and some peanut butter or oats. You control exactly what goes in.

Ask us which gainers are in stock — we carry brands including MuscleTech and Muscle Gears, alongside a wide range of whey. Tell us your weight, your appetite and your training, and we will help you choose.

If you have diabetes or any other medical condition, speak to your doctor before using a high-calorie supplement.

props.heading: Just joined a gym? The only supplements a beginner needs
props.body:
If you have just joined a gym, the supplement shelf can feel like a test you did not study for. Here is the honest short version: most beginners need very little.

FIRST: FOOD, SLEEP AND TRAINING
No powder makes up for skipped meals, short nights or missed sessions. Get those three right and you will make progress. Supplements are the last few per cent.

THE ONE MOST BEGINNERS FIND USEFUL: PROTEIN
If you struggle to eat enough protein from food, a whey protein is the simplest way to close the gap. One scoop a day, after training or with a meal, is where most people start. Our guide to whey versus isolate will help you choose.

THE ONE WORTH CONSIDERING: CREATINE
Creatine monohydrate is one of the most studied supplements for strength training, and it is inexpensive. A small daily dose is all it takes. Read our creatine guide first.

THE ONES THAT CAN WAIT
Pre-workouts, fat burners, BCAAs and long lists of "stacks" are not where a beginner should spend money. If your diet already has enough protein, BCAAs add little. Pre-workouts are high in caffeine; if you are sensitive to it, avoid them.

A SENSIBLE FIRST SHOPPING LIST
• A whey protein, in a flavour you like.
• Optionally, a creatine monohydrate.
• A shaker.
That is it.

HOW TO SPEND WISELY
• Compare the cost per serving, not the price of the tub.
• Try a smaller pack of a new flavour first.
• Buy from a shop that sells sealed, genuine stock — see our guide on spotting a genuine supplement.

At Protein Basket we would rather sell you the two things you need than the ten you do not. Come in, tell us your goal, and we will keep it simple.

A note on health: supplements are not medicines. If you have a medical condition, take regular medication, are pregnant or breastfeeding, or are under 18, speak to your doctor before you start.

items.q: Should I buy whey or whey isolate?
